passage:
Lalremsiami had been happy with her phone for two years. Then, during the Christmas fair in Aizawl, Vidya posted a photo taken with the newest model, the camera glowing. Lalremsiami's own screen had a crack across one corner, and her data was nearly used up until the first of the month. The power had been out since morning, so she could only scroll on her last bit of battery.
Every post seemed to show something better. Her phone, which had taken a lovely photo of the lantern yesterday, suddenly felt like a stone.
"Can I get a new phone?" she asked her mother.
"Fees are due this month."
Lalremsiami said nothing and turned the phone over. Nothing about it had changed. She only noticed she felt small.

qa.q: What was wrong with Lalremsiami's own screen?
qa.a: It had a crack across one corner.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling as she scrolled through the posts?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt inadequate and small. The phone that had felt fine suddenly felt like a stone once she compared it with other people's posts.

qa.q: What small step could Lalremsiami try when the comparison feeling arrives?
qa.a: She could put the phone down and look at what it still does for her, like taking the lantern photo, and choose a moment to stop scrolling.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami's mother have felt hearing the request for a new phone while fees are due?
qa.a: Lalremsiami's mother probably felt stretched and worried about money, and maybe sorry to have to refuse.

grounding: A teenager who was fine with her phone feels lacking after seeing friends' posts, though nothing about the phone has changed.

passage:
Usha had been proud of her 78 per cent all week. She had even bought her mum a sweet from her own savings to celebrate. At lunch on Monday her phone lit up with Sahil's story: "91%!! 🎉", and a dozen friends replied with fireworks.
She looked at the number for a long time. Then at the report card in her bag, which hadn't changed by a single digit. "It's just marks," she told herself, but her lunch tasted like paper.
That night she opened the app again and scrolled past three more numbers. By the time she shut it, 78 felt like a failure she had invented herself.

qa.q: What mark did Usha get?
qa.a: Usha got 78 per cent.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as her lunch tasted like paper?
qa.a: Usha felt deflated and inadequate, though her own mark was exactly what it was that morning.

qa.q: What could Usha do to bring back her earlier contentment?
qa.a: Usha could take a break from the app and remember what she worked on for the 78. She could also talk to her mum about it.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt posting the mark?
qa.a: Sahil was probably proud and excited, since a dozen friends were cheering. Sahil may not have thought about how others would feel seeing it.

grounding: A teenager who was fine with her marks feels lacking after seeing a friend's post, though her result has not changed.

passage:
"Suraj, you've been scrolling with that long face for an hour," said Charu masi, pouring tea. "Let me tell you something. When I was sixteen, I was happy with my one good salwar and my second-division marks. Then my friend Anju came back from her cousin's wedding in Bombay with a stack of photos. New clothes, a big hotel, everyone smiling.
That night my salwar looked old. My marks looked small. My room looked dull. But nothing had changed! Same room, same clothes. Only the photos.
For weeks I compared everything. I stopped enjoying my Sunday music class. Finally my father asked why I'd gone quiet, and I said, 'Everyone else has more.' He said, 'Did you have less yesterday?' I laughed, and it broke a little.
So, Suraj. What's changed in your life since this morning? Nothing, na?"

qa.q: Where had Anju come back from?
qa.a: From her cousin's wedding in Bombay.

qa.q: How did young Charu feel after seeing Anju's photos?
qa.a: She felt lacking and dissatisfied, as if her salwar, marks and room had suddenly become old and dull.

qa.q: What turning point in the story helped Charu masi?
qa.a: Her father's question, 'Did you have less yesterday?', which made her see nothing had actually changed except the comparison.

qa.q: How might Anju have seen the photos she shared?
qa.a: Anju probably just wanted to share a happy trip, without knowing they would make her friend feel lacking.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how comparing herself with a friend's photos made her feel lacking though nothing had changed.

passage: It was exam week, the building had power cuts every evening, and Bhupen was down to his last gigabyte of data. He'd been perfectly happy with his old phone, cracked corner and all. It did everything he needed. Then, during a power cut, he opened his feed by torchlight. Noor had posted her new phone, photos from a hill trip, and a caption: "blessed." Three other classmates had new phones too. Bhupen looked down at his cracked corner. Suddenly it felt embarrassing. He spent twenty minutes looking at phone prices instead of revising, and went to bed feeling poor and grumpy. In the morning, the power was back. His old phone woke him at six, as always. He looked at it and thought, "Nothing's actually different from last week." He deleted the app for exam week.

qa.q: What did Noor's caption say?
qa.a: Blessed.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling after looking at the posts?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, poor and grumpy, as if his phone had suddenly become not good enough.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the app for exam week worked, because it stopped the comparison that was creating dissatisfaction and wasting revision time.

qa.q: How might Noor have seen her own post?
qa.a: Noor probably just wanted to share a happy moment, without imagining it would make Bhupen feel lacking.

grounding: Shows a teenager happy with his phone until friends' posts make him feel lacking, though nothing had actually changed.

passage: Karthik got his Class 11 half-yearly results in the evening: 82 per cent. He was pleased. He'd worked hard on chemistry, and it showed. Amma made payasam. Then, at nine, the class group lit up. Tanvir posted his marksheet: 95 per cent. Then others: 91, 93, 89. Congratulations poured in. Karthik put the phone down, then picked it up again. By ten, his 82 looked tiny. He stopped replying to messages and didn't finish the payasam. In the morning, Appa asked why he looked so glum. "My marks are bad." Appa frowned. "Last night you were happy. What changed?" Karthik opened his mouth to answer and found he couldn't. The number was the same. The chemistry was the same. Only the group chat had happened. He sighed and pushed his phone into the drawer.

qa.q: What percentage did Tanvir post?
qa.a: 95 per cent.

qa.q: What was Karthik feeling by ten o'clock?
qa.a: He felt dissatisfied and glum, his 82 looking tiny after seeing everyone's marks.

qa.q: What small step could Karthik take the next time results come out?
qa.a: He could enjoy his own result with family first and mute the class group for a day, so comparisons don't spoil it.

qa.q: How might Appa see Karthik's change of mood?
qa.a: Appa is puzzled, since nothing changed from the night before when Karthik was happy.

grounding: Shows a teenager who was pleased with his marks until friends' posts made him feel lacking, though nothing had actually changed.

passage:
"Aadhya, you were dancing at lunch. What happened?"
"Nothing. I'm fine."
"You've been scrolling for an hour. That's not fine."
"Everyone's posting results. Riddhi got ninety-four. Tushar got ninety-six. There's a whole class story with topper stickers."
"And you got eighty-two. Which you said was your best ever. At lunch."
"That was before."
"Before what? Your marks didn't change."
Aadhya stared at the phone. "I know. It just feels smaller now."
Afreen held out her hand. "Give it to me for ten minutes. Tell me what you were dancing about."
Aadhya hesitated, then handed it over. "Maths. I finally got over seventy in maths."
"See? That's still true."
Aadhya laughed a little. "Yeah. It is."

qa.q: What did Aadhya score overall?
qa.a: She got eighty-two.

qa.q: How did Aadhya feel after scrolling through the result posts?
qa.a: She felt deflated and inadequate, as if her marks had shrunk, even though nothing had changed.

qa.q: Which step helped Aadhya reconnect with her own result?
qa.a: Putting the phone away for ten minutes and saying what she had been proud of, like getting over seventy in maths.

qa.q: How does Afreen see Aadhya's sudden change?
qa.a: Afreen sees clearly that the marks are the same and only the comparison changed, and she wants Aadhya's joy back.

grounding: Shows a teenager happy with her marks until friends' posts make her feel lacking, although nothing has actually changed.
